Hoffmann's two-toed sloth (Choloepus hoffmanni) exhibits a suite of life-history traits that are remarkably slow-paced even among xenarthrans. Neonates are relatively large, with a measured wet weight at birth of 402 grams [Wwb = 402 grams], a substantial initial investment that reflects the species' high degree of altriciality followed by prolonged maternal care. This sizable newborn mass is consistent with the broader pattern observed in sloths, where a single precocial or semi-precocial offspring is the norm. The gestating embryo develops over an extended period; gestation time in this species has been documented at 350 days [tg = 350 days] under the stable thermal conditions of their rainforest habitat, maintained at approximately 34.4 °C [T = 34.4 °C]. This lengthy gestation, comparable to that of much larger ungulates, is thought to be linked to the sloth's exceptionally low metabolic rate and the energetic constraints imposed by its folivorous diet.

Reproductive output in Hoffmann's sloth is extraordinarily low, a pattern typical of arboreal folivores facing limited energy availability. Females produce a single pup per litter [N_R_i = single pup per litter] and, under the typical ambient conditions of their environment at 34.4 °C [T = 34.4 °C], they achieve only about one litter every 456 days [F_R_i = about one litter every 456 days]. This extraordinarily slow reproductive pace, equating to less than one offspring per year, places Choloepus hoffmanni among the least fecund mammals of its body size. The lengthy interval between births is partly explained by the extended period of maternal dependency following parturition, during which the calf clings to the mother's fur and nurses for many months before achieving nutritional independence. Such a low reproductive rate is consistent with the energy-conserving lifestyle characteristic of sloths, which subsist on a low-calorie diet of leaves and require extended periods for digestion and metabolic processing.

The protracted developmental schedule of the sloth is further emphasized by the significant time elapsed between birth and the complete cessation of nursing. Specifically, the time since birth at weaning has been recorded as 21 days since birth [tx = 21 days since birth] in this species, although this figure likely represents the age at which solid food is first sampled rather than full nutritional independence at a temperature of 34.4 °C [T = 34.4 °C]. The actual period of maternal milk dependency and close physical association extends far longer, with juveniles remaining with their mothers for a substantial portion of their early life. This extended lactation period is energetically costly for the female, contributing to the lengthy inter-birth interval. Physiological work conducted at 34.4 °C [T = 34.4 °C] has measured a maximum basal metabolic rate of 799 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 799 milliliters of oxygen per hour], a value that is conspicuously low even for a mammal of its size and underscores the energetic foundation of its slow life history.

Ontogenetic development proceeds very gradually, with puberty delayed accordingly. The time since birth at puberty is estimated at 730 days since birth [tp = 730 days since birth] under the species' typical thermal regime of 34.4 °C [T = 34.4 °C], meaning that females do not attain sexual maturity until well into their second year. This late maturation, combined with the low reproductive rate, contributes to a life history strategy optimized for high adult survival. Adult females ultimately reach an asymptotic or maximum body mass of around 8,000 grams [Wwi = around 8,000 grams], although field measurements indicate considerable individual variation, with a recorded range of 2.1 to 9 kilograms. This mass is attained gradually, reflecting the slow growth rates that are characteristic of species with very low resting metabolic expenditures.

Lifespan in this species is comparatively long, consistent with its position on the slow end of the mammalian life-history continuum. Maximum longevity has been estimated at approximately 41 years [am = approximately 41 years] when individuals are maintained at 34.4 °C [T = 34.4 °C], a figure approaching that of some primates of far greater body size. This extended lifespan allows for multiple reproductive opportunities across a female's lifetime, partially offsetting the exceedingly low annual fecundity. The interplay between a 350-day gestation (350 days) [tg = 350 days] and a long post-reproductive period for senescent individuals in captivity suggests that natural mortality in the wild is likely driven more by predation or disease than by intrinsic senescence at a temperature of 34.4 °C [T = 34.4 °C]. The remarkable longevity, combined with the minimal daily energetic expenditure reflected in the basal oxygen consumption, makes this species a compelling model for studying the physiological underpinnings of slow aging.
